profile.name: Jay Dhangar
profile.headline: I engineer AI systems for production.
profile.sub: LLM applications end to end: orchestration, retrieval, guardrails, evaluation, and the backend that runs them.
profile.summary: Software Engineer specializing in Agentic AI and Automation, with hands-on experience building autonomous and multi-agent systems using LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, and Agno. Strong background in workflow automation, API integrations, and multimodal AI including OCR, image generation, video creation, and TTS.

systems.name: ChristianAI
systems.summary: A dual-path AI assistant that handles both Christian-specific and general ChatGPT-style conversations, with web-grounded answers, image generation, and narrated scripture.
systems.problem: Build one assistant that safely serves two very different intents (faith questions and everyday requests), answers with current web-grounded information, supports scripture narration and AI-generated posters, and keeps model costs aligned with what users actually consume.
highlights: Architected a dual-path AI assistant supporting Christian-specific and general conversations using OpenAI APIs with intent classification and safety guardrails.
Integrated the OpenAI Responses API with live web search to provide current, web-grounded answers with citations.
Implemented an LLM-based query-classification fallback to improve intent detection for misspellings and ambiguous queries.
Built AI image-generation and vision workflows with GPT-4o / GPT-4o-mini, including poster generation and intelligent person placement.
Developed a face-compositing pipeline that integrates user-uploaded photos into AI-generated poster designs.
Built AI Bible narration infrastructure using TTS and Whisper, generating synchronized audio.
Designed and implemented the complete Bible Player backend, serving over 100,000 users.
Re-engineered billing from chapter-based charging to real listening-time usage metering.
Built automated narration caching jobs, improving first-play performance and reducing wait times.
Recalibrated the credit/pricing infrastructure based on actual OpenAI usage costs.
Designed a 90-day no-repeat devotional system with timezone-aware daily verse selection.
Implemented a 30-day quiz-streak reward system to improve retention.
Implemented semantic AI-generated conversation titles.
Developed a scripture-translation quality system for consistent multilingual poster generation.

decisions.title: Classify intent before generating
decisions.why: Two assistant behaviors share one entry point. Routing first gives each path its own prompts and guardrails instead of one prompt trying to do both.

decisions.title: LLM classification as a fallback, not the default
decisions.why: Clear queries take the primary path; the extra model call is reserved for misspelled or ambiguous input, where it adds the most.

decisions.title: Web search through the Responses API, with citations
decisions.why: Current information changes after training; citations let users check the answer themselves.

decisions.title: Pre-generate narration
decisions.why: Caching jobs move TTS generation off the user's first play.

decisions.title: Meter what users consume
decisions.why: Billing moved from chapters to listening time, and credit pricing was recalibrated from actual OpenAI spend.

systems.result: In production with a Bible Player backend used by over 100,000 users, web-grounded chat with citations, narrated scripture, and personalized poster generation.

systems.name: Mendle
systems.summary: A mental-wellness and mentorship platform with a resilient LLM orchestration layer, quality-validated responses, and privacy-preserving multi-party AI mediation.
systems.problem: Sensitive wellness and mentorship conversations need an LLM layer that stays up under provider rate limits, stays relevant over long conversations, grounds itself in current information without opening an injection hole, and protects participant privacy in multi-party sessions.
highlights: Built the core LLM orchestration layer using Groq and LangChain, with retry/backoff and differentiated per-minute vs. daily token-limit handling.
Implemented embedding-based response-quality validation using cosine-similarity relevance scoring, repetition checks, and length validation.
Integrated real-time web-search grounding via Serper / Google Search API with prompt-injection defenses.
Designed a privacy-preserving multi-party AI mediation engine that controls participant anonymity in sensitive conversations.
Developed recency-aware context management, improving conversation coherence and relevance.
Built an Emotional Memory Object pipeline that generates insights from conversations.
Implemented AI oversight tracking model latency and user interaction metrics.

decisions.title: Separate per-minute from daily token limits
decisions.why: A per-minute limit clears within seconds and is worth retrying; a daily limit won't, so retrying it only adds latency and load.

decisions.title: Validate every response before delivery
decisions.why: Relevance, repetition, and length are measurable, so they are checked with embeddings and rules instead of assumed.

decisions.title: Treat search results as untrusted input
decisions.why: Web content can carry instructions aimed at the model. Grounding without injection defenses turns retrieval into an attack surface.

decisions.title: Weight context by recency
decisions.why: Recent turns carry the most signal for coherence in long conversations.

decisions.title: Enforce anonymity in the mediation engine
decisions.why: In multi-party conversations, privacy is controlled by the system rather than left to model behavior.

systems.result: A production orchestration layer on Groq and LangChain with fault-tolerant generation, embedding-validated responses, injection-aware search grounding, and latency and interaction monitoring.

systems.name: ResuMate AI + JobHunt AI
systems.summary: Two AI products on one FastAPI backend: a multi-agent resume builder, and a job-search aggregator with scam scoring, RAG resume matching, and AI-drafted applications.
systems.problem: Build and tailor a resume, find real jobs across many boards, spot scam postings, and apply, all in one app that keeps working when no paid AI keys are configured.
highlights: Designed a multi-agent backend: eight specialized agents (resume reading with OCR, template search and parsing, uploaded templates, natural-language editing, generation, export, job search) under a coordinator that owns version and prompt history.

Built RAG job matching: the resume and live postings are embedded with OpenAI text-embedding-3-small and re-ranked by cosine similarity blended with skill overlap, with a pure-Python TF-IDF fallback offline.

Built JobHunt's parallel fan-out across job boards with cross-board dedupe, whole-word relevance matching, and a 0-100 genuineness score with visible reasons (apply domain, HTTPS, scam wording, salary plausibility, posting age).
Added an anti-data-loss guard to LLM-powered natural-language resume edits, with a rule-based offline fallback.
Made job alerts quota-aware: a ~20h persistent cache for identical searches and a monthly API budget that hard-stops before the free tier runs out.
Offline export to PDF, DOCX, HTML, PNG, Markdown, and JSON in pure Python; pluggable MongoDB / SQLite storage with automatic fallback.
Built a portfolio-website generator that renders a resume into five hand-built, self-contained designs.
Covered the backend with a 62-test pytest suite running in CI.

decisions.title: Every AI feature has a no-key fallback
decisions.why: Embeddings fall back to TF-IDF, fit analysis and emails to deterministic heuristics and templates, edits to rule-based logic. The app stays usable without paid keys.

decisions.title: Provider-agnostic LLM layer
decisions.why: LLM_PROVIDER=auto uses whichever of OpenAI, Anthropic, or Gemini is configured, so no feature is locked to one vendor.

decisions.title: Aggregators instead of automated logins
decisions.why: Automated LinkedIn or Naukri logins violate those sites' terms; aggregator APIs index the same postings legitimately.

decisions.title: Budget-capped external APIs
decisions.why: A persistent cache plus a monthly hard stop keeps scheduled alerts from exhausting a free tier.

decisions.title: Pluggable storage with fallback
decisions.why: MongoDB when configured, zero-config SQLite otherwise, and automatic fallback if MongoDB is unreachable at startup.

systems.result: Open-source app with a documented REST API, 62 backend tests in CI, and RAG matching that costs about $0.00007 per run with embeddings.

systems.name: Multi-Agent AI Recruitment Assistant
systems.summary: A multi-agent system that ingests resumes straight from Gmail, scores candidates against job requirements, and triggers recruitment emails automatically.
systems.problem: Screening resumes that arrive by email is manual: reading each one, comparing it to the role, shortlisting, and following up.
highlights: Built a multi-agent system that auto-ingests resumes from Gmail and converts them to structured data.
Matched candidate skills against job requirements using LLM-based scoring and analysis.
Split the workflow across collaborating agents for resume screening, candidate shortlisting, and interview scheduling.
Triggered automated recruitment emails via LangGraph orchestration pipelines.

decisions.title: One agent per responsibility
decisions.why: Screening, shortlisting, and scheduling take different inputs and produce different outputs; separate agents keep each prompt narrow.

decisions.title: Structure before scoring
decisions.why: Resumes are converted to structured fields first, so matching compares like with like.

decisions.title: Explicit orchestration with LangGraph
decisions.why: Handoffs between agents are defined as a graph, which makes the sequence inspectable.

systems.result: Automates the path from a resume in the inbox to a recruitment email.

systems.name: AI Media & Content Generation Suite
systems.summary: An automation suite that turns images and text into extracted data, generated visuals, and ready-to-post social content.
systems.problem: Turning raw images and text into usable content (extracted text, generated visuals, channel-specific posts) normally takes several manual tools.
highlights: Designed OCR-based automation pipelines to extract and process text from images using LLMs.
Built text-to-image generation workflows using Stable Diffusion.
Automated multi-platform social media content generation from image and text inputs.
Extended the suite with AI marketing-video generation and blog-to-speech TTS.

decisions.title: OCR first, LLM second
decisions.why: OCR extracts the raw text; the LLM then structures and rewrites it, so each tool does the part it is good at.

decisions.title: Per-channel output
decisions.why: One input produces posts tailored to each social channel instead of one generic caption.

systems.result: One workflow from an image or prompt to extracted text, generated images, and channel-ready posts.

systems.name: Jay.OS
systems.summary: This site: a static portfolio whose content lives in one JSON file, plus a RAG assistant that answers questions about it with citations.
systems.problem: A portfolio that describes AI engineering is weaker evidence than one that runs it. Visitors should be able to question the work directly and get grounded, cited answers.
highlights: Single source of truth: every section and the assistant's knowledge base are generated from one portfolio.json.
BM25 retrieval with weighted query expansion, shared by the browser and the serverless function.
A serverless /api/ask endpoint grounds a Groq LLM in the retrieved passages with a cite-your-sources prompt.
Degrades gracefully: without an API key or network, the browser answers extractively from the same passages.
Every answer shows its retrieval trace and the systems it drew from.

decisions.title: Lexical retrieval instead of embeddings
decisions.why: The corpus is small, curated, and keyword-dense. BM25 runs in the browser with no model or vector store, and its rankings are easy to inspect and debug.

decisions.title: One retrieval implementation for client and server
decisions.why: The local fallback and the LLM path retrieve identical context, so their answers can't silently diverge.

decisions.title: Fallback as a first-class mode
decisions.why: The assistant still answers when the LLM is unavailable, and says which mode it's in.

systems.result: Live on Vercel. Every answer is traceable to the passages it used.

lab.title: Synonyms outranked the entity
lab.problem: Ask Jay.OS ranks portfolio passages with BM25 before answering.
lab.failure: “Explain the architecture of ChristianAI” ranked the Media Suite and Mendle diagrams above ChristianAI's. “Does he know Kubernetes” matched an unrelated passage.
lab.rootCause: Query expansion added synonyms at full weight, so generic terms outscored the one entity the visitor named. “know” wasn't a stop word.
lab.fix: Weighted expansions at 0.45 of the visitor's own terms, strengthened title matches, trimmed the architecture aliases, and added conversational filler to the stop list.
lab.lesson: Retrieval fails silently. Test with real questions and check what ranks first.

lab.title: The API the agent needed wasn't reachable
lab.problem: Build an AI agent that creates TikTok ads through the TikTok Ads API.
lab.failure: Live Ads API access was unavailable: the OAuth authorization could not complete.
lab.rootCause: TikTok Ads uses OAuth with PKCE requirements and regional restrictions that blocked authorization for this app.
lab.fix: A mocked OAuth access token simulates authenticated requests to exercise error handling and retry decisions; conversation and ad configuration persist in state.json for deterministic, resumable runs.
lab.lesson: When an external API is out of reach, build against a faithful stand-in and make the agent's state resumable.

lab.title: Typos broke intent detection
lab.problem: One assistant serves two intents, Christian-specific and general, and has to route each message to the right path.
lab.failure: Misspelled and ambiguous queries weren't detected reliably, so they could land on the wrong assistant path.
lab.rootCause: The primary classifier depends on recognizable phrasing; typos and vague wording fall outside it.
lab.fix: An LLM-based classification fallback takes over for queries the primary classifier can't resolve.
lab.lesson: Keep the predictable path for clear input and escalate to a model only for the hard cases.

lab.title: First play waited on TTS
lab.problem: Scripture narration is generated with TTS so users can listen to any chapter.
lab.failure: First plays were slow: the user waited while narration was produced.
lab.rootCause: Audio generation sat on the user's critical path at first request.
lab.fix: Automated narration caching jobs pre-generate audio, so first play is served from cache.
lab.lesson: If output is predictable, generate it before anyone asks for it.

lab.title: Billing didn't match consumption
lab.problem: Credits pay for narrated listening, and credit prices have to cover model costs.
lab.failure: Chapter-based charging didn't reflect how much users actually listened, and credit pricing didn't track real OpenAI usage costs.
lab.rootCause: The billing unit (a chapter) and the pricing assumptions weren't tied to real consumption or real spend.
lab.fix: Re-engineered billing to meter real listening time and recalibrated credit pricing against actual OpenAI usage costs.
lab.lesson: Bill in the unit users consume, and price from measured cost, not estimates.

lab.title: Two rate limits, one error
lab.problem: Every Mendle response depends on a Groq call, and the provider enforces both per-minute and daily token limits.
lab.failure: Handled as one generic error, a rate limit either breaks the conversation or triggers retries that can never succeed.
lab.rootCause: Per-minute and daily limits look alike but recover on completely different timescales.
lab.fix: Retry with backoff for per-minute limits; daily-limit errors are distinguished and handled without pointless retries.
lab.lesson: A retry policy is only as good as its error taxonomy. Classify failures before reacting to them.

lab.title: Fluent isn't relevant
lab.problem: In wellness conversations, an off-topic or repetitive reply is a real failure, not a cosmetic one.
lab.failure: Generated responses can drift off-topic, repeat earlier replies, or come out the wrong length while still sounding fluent.
lab.rootCause: The generator doesn't check its own output against the conversation.
lab.fix: An embedding-based quality gate on every response: cosine-similarity relevance scoring, repetition checks, and length validation.
lab.lesson: Anything you can score, score before it reaches the user.

lab.title: Retrieved text can give orders
lab.problem: Grounding responses in live web search keeps answers current.
lab.failure: Search results are third-party text; instructions embedded in them could be followed by the model.
lab.rootCause: Retrieved content enters the same context window as trusted instructions.
lab.fix: Prompt-injection defenses on the Serper / Google Search grounding path.
lab.lesson: Retrieval widens the attack surface. Treat retrieved text as data, never as instructions.

lab.title: An edit that deletes too much
lab.problem: Users edit resumes in plain language: “Replace C++ with Rust”, “Remove internship”.
lab.failure: An LLM rewriting a structured resume can silently drop or change content the user never asked to touch.
lab.rootCause: A generative edit rewrites the document, not just the requested part.
lab.fix: An anti-data-loss guard around LLM edits, plus a rule-based fallback when no model is configured.
lab.lesson: When an LLM edits user data, verify what changed, not just that it responded.

lab.title: Scheduled searches vs. a free tier
lab.problem: Job alerts run on a schedule against a job-search API with a limited free tier.
lab.failure: Repeated and scheduled searches can exhaust the monthly quota, after which the source stops returning results.
lab.rootCause: Every identical search is a new billable call, and nothing caps total monthly usage.
lab.fix: A ~20h persistent cache shared by identical searches, alerts capped at once per day, and a monthly budget (default 180 calls) that hard-stops before the free tier runs out.
lab.lesson: External quotas are a design constraint. Build the budget into the system.

architectures.name: ChristianAI assistant pipeline
architectures.caption: Queries are classified (with an LLM fallback for messy input), routed to the right assistant, grounded with live web search, and returned with citations.

nodes.label: User message
nodes.what: A chat message from the app: a faith question or an everyday request.
nodes.why: One entry point for both assistant modes.
fails: Misspellings and vague phrasing make intent unclear

nodes.label: Intent classifier
nodes.what: Decides whether a message needs the Christian-specific or the general assistant.
nodes.why: The two paths need different prompts, sources, and guardrails.
fails: Misroutes typos and ambiguous queries, which the LLM fallback catches

nodes.label: LLM fallback classifier
nodes.what: An LLM classification step for queries the primary classifier can't resolve.
nodes.why: Improves intent detection for misspellings and ambiguous queries.
fails: Adds latency and cost whenever it's triggered

nodes.label: Safety guardrails
nodes.what: Constrains what each assistant path is allowed to answer.
nodes.why: A faith-focused product needs predictable, safe behavior in both modes.
fails: Over-blocking legitimate questions
New phrasing slipping past rules

nodes.label: Christian-specific path
nodes.what: Handles faith questions with Christian-specific behavior and framing.
nodes.why: Domain answers need domain context.
fails: Tone or instructions leaking between paths

nodes.label: General assistant path
nodes.what: ChatGPT-style help for everyday requests.
nodes.why: Users get one app for both kinds of question.
fails: Faith questions misrouted here lose their domain framing

nodes.label: OpenAI Responses API
nodes.what: Generates the answer and can call tools such as web search.
nodes.why: Generation and tool use through one API.
fails: Provider latency and timeouts

nodes.why: Answers about recent events need current data, with citations users can check.

Untrusted text entering the prompt

nodes.label: GPT-4o vision / images
nodes.what: Poster generation, person placement, and face compositing of user photos.
nodes.why: Lets users create shareable scripture posters with their own photos.
fails: Generative models can distort faces
Scripture text inconsistent across languages, handled by a translation quality system

nodes.label: Answer + citations
nodes.what: The final response with its sources.
nodes.why: Users can verify web-grounded claims.
fails: A citation that doesn't support the claim it's attached to

nodes.label: Semantic title
nodes.what: An AI-generated conversation title based on meaning.
nodes.why: Makes chat history navigable.
fails: Generic titles that don't distinguish conversations

nodes.label: Usage-metered credits

nodes.why: Credits track what users consume and what models actually cost.

architectures.name: Mendle orchestration layer

nodes.label: Conversation turn

nodes.why: Every response starts from the latest turn.
fails: Sensitive content that needs careful handling end to end

History outgrowing the token budget

nodes.label: Anonymity controls

nodes.why: Privacy is enforced by the system, not left to the model.

nodes.label: Serper / Google Search
nodes.what: Real-time web search for grounding.
nodes.why: Keeps responses current.
fails: Irrelevant results
Added latency

nodes.label: Prompt-injection defenses
nodes.what: Treats retrieved web content as untrusted data.
nodes.why: Search results can contain instructions aimed at the model.
fails: New injection patterns that bypass defenses

nodes.label: Groq + LangChain
nodes.what: The core LLM orchestration layer.
nodes.why: Fast inference with a composable pipeline.
fails: Rate limits
Provider errors

nodes.label: Retry / backoff
nodes.what: Retries transient failures with increasing delays.
nodes.why: Transient per-minute limits clear quickly.
fails: Retry storms without a bound on attempts

nodes.label: Token-limit handling
nodes.what: Distinguishes per-minute from daily token-limit errors.
nodes.why: They recover on different timescales, so they need different responses.

nodes.label: Embedding relevance
nodes.what: Scores response relevance with cosine similarity against the conversation.
nodes.why: Catches off-topic replies before users see them.
fails: Thresholds too strict reject good answers; too loose let drift through

nodes.label: Repetition + length checks
nodes.what: Rejects responses that repeat earlier replies or fall outside length bounds.
nodes.why: Repetition and rambling are measurable defects.
fails: Legitimate restatement flagged as repetition

nodes.label: Latency metrics
nodes.what: Tracks model latency.
nodes.why: Surfaces slowdowns and regressions.
fails: Averages hiding tail latency

nodes.label: Interaction metrics
nodes.what: Tracks how users interact with responses.
nodes.why: Grounds improvements in real usage.
fails: Metrics that don't reflect real user outcomes

thinking.title: Guardrails are part of the product
thinking.body: Safety isn't a layer bolted on at the end. Intent classification, safety guardrails, and prompt-injection defenses shape what a system is allowed to do from the first request.
evidence: injection defenses and anonymity controls in Mendle
reasoning: A guardrail added after launch is a patch on behavior users have already seen. Deciding what a system may do, which intents it serves and which content it trusts, belongs in the architecture.

In practice that means classifying before generating (ChristianAI's intent routing), treating retrieved text as data (Mendle's injection defenses), and enforcing privacy in the system rather than in a prompt (Mendle's anonymity controls).

thinking.title: Assume the model will fail
thinking.body: Rate limits, timeouts, and ambiguous input are normal operating conditions. Systems should retry, back off, and fall back instead of breaking.
evidence: Retry/backoff with per-minute vs. daily limit handling
reasoning: LLM providers rate-limit, time out, and return unexpected output as a matter of course. The question isn't whether a call fails, but whether the product degrades gracefully when it does.

The useful move is classifying failures: a per-minute limit deserves a retry, a daily limit doesn't. The same idea runs through ResuMate, where every AI feature has a deterministic fallback, and this site, which answers locally when the LLM is unavailable.

thinking.title: Measure quality, don't eyeball it
thinking.body: If a response can be scored, score it. Relevance, repetition, and latency are numbers you can track and improve.
reasoning: Looking good in a demo doesn't survive real conversations. Relevance, repetition, and length can be computed on every response, so they should be.
Measurement applies to retrieval too: this site's assistant ranked the wrong architecture first until it was tested with real questions and the top result was checked.

thinking.title: Ground every answer
thinking.body: Models are most useful when they're connected to current, verifiable sources, and honest about what they don't know.
reasoning: A model's knowledge is frozen and unattributed. Grounding, whether web search or retrieval over known data, makes answers current and checkable, and citations let the user do the checking.
Grounding has costs: retrieved text is untrusted, and bad retrieval produces confident wrong answers. So grounding ships with injection defenses and retrieval tests.

thinking.title: Cost is an engineering constraint
thinking.body: Token spend, caching, and billing models are design decisions. Pricing should follow real usage, not guesses.
reasoning: Model calls, TTS generation, and third-party APIs cost money per use, so the billing unit, the cache, and the quota are part of the design, not an afterthought.

ChristianAI moved to listening-time metering and recalibrated pricing on measured OpenAI cost; JobHunt caps its job API with a persistent cache and a monthly budget; narration is pre-generated so cost and latency aren't paid on the user's first play.
